lines.text: Why does solid iodine melt readily while diamond does not, although both contain covalent bonds? The answer lies in which particles make the crystal.

Crystalline solids have repeating lattices. Giant ionic lattices contain oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction, N ay C L has sodium plus and chloride, M G O has magnesium two plus and oxide. Simple molecular lattices contain discrete molecules held by intermolecular forces, iodine has I two molecules, buckminsterfullerene has C sixty cages, and ice has H two O molecules hydrogen bonded in an open lattice. Giant molecular, giant covalent, lattices are continuous covalent networks, each silicon in S I O two bonds to four O atoms, each O bridges two silicon, diamond has four bonds per carbon, graphite has three bonds per carbon in layers and delocalised electrons. Giant metallic lattices, such as copper, contain positive metal ions attracted to delocalised electrons.
Classifying the particles first tells you which attractions melting must overcome and which charge carriers might move.

Giant ionic, alternating ions, strong electrostatic attraction. Simple molecular, separate molecules, intermolecular forces. Giant molecular, continuous covalent network. Giant metallic, positive ions and delocalised electrons.
Why is C sixty molecular even though each cage contains many covalent bonds?
Two high melting solids may conduct differently. Their melting points describe attraction strength, while their conductivity reveals whether charge can move.

Explain melting and boiling points by the attractions overcome, molecular solids lose intermolecular forces, while giant lattices disrupt strong ionic, metallic or network covalent bonds. Ionic solids have fixed ions and do not conduct as solids, but molten or dissolved ions move and conduct. Metals conduct in both solid and liquid states through delocalised electrons. Graphite conducts along layers through delocalised electrons, diamond and S I O two lack mobile charge carriers. Solubility depends on whether solvent solute interactions can compensate for disrupting the original structure. Many ionic solids dissolve in water by ion hydration, but M G O is only sparingly soluble. Iodine is poorly soluble in water, giant covalent networks are generally insoluble. Predict each property from the particular structure and bonding, rather than from one label alone.
Conduction tests distinguish fixed ions from mobile ions or electrons, solubility and melting point then strengthen the interpretation.

Melting a molecular solid overcomes intermolecular forces. Ionic melts and solutions conduct through mobile ions. Metals conduct through delocalised electrons. Solubility depends on solvent interactions, not a universal rule.
Why does molten N ay C L conduct while solid N ay C L does not?
An unknown material gives clues rather than its identity. A pattern of properties can reveal the particles and bonding in its lattice.

Deduce structure and bonding by combining evidence. Low melting or boiling point and poor conductivity in every state suggest discrete molecules with intermolecular forces. High melting point, no solid conduction and good molten conduction suggest a giant ionic lattice, ions become mobile on melting. Conductivity in solid and liquid plus malleability indicates giant metallic bonding with mobile delocalised electrons. A very high melting point, insolubility and no conduction usually indicate a giant covalent network, graphite is the important conducting layered exception. Water solubility can support an ionic deduction but is not decisive, because some ionic solids are sparingly soluble and some molecular substances dissolve or react in water. Explain how each observation supports the conclusion.
This uses the same particle and mobility reasoning as property prediction, now in reverse.
Compare solid and liquid conductivity first. Use melting point, solubility and malleability as further evidence. State the structure and the mobile or fixed particles that justify it.
A brittle high melting solid conducts only after melting. What structure is most likely, and why?
Which oxide has a simple structure rather than a giant structure?
P four O ten consists of discrete molecules, M G O and ay L two O three are giant ionic, while S I O two is giant covalent. Option C wrongly treats network S I O two as molecular.
Which solid has a simple molecular lattice?
Sulfur forms discrete S eight molecules in a molecular lattice. Calcium fluoride is ionic, nickel metallic and silicon of IV oxide giant covalent.
This question is about buckminsterfullerene, graphite, iodine and diamond. How many of these substances have a simple molecular structure?
Buckminsterfullerene and iodine are simple molecular, graphite and diamond are giant covalent. Option B misses one of the two molecular solids.
In which carbon allotrope are all electrons localised?
Diamond uses all four carbon valence electrons in localised covalent bonds. Graphite and graphene have delocalised electrons, as does buckminsterfullerene within each molecule.
Solid carbon dioxide, C O two, is similar to solid iodine, I two, in its structure. Which statement about solid C O two and solid S I O two is correct?
Both solids have orderly lattices, but C O two is molecular and S I O two is giant covalent. Option B incorrectly assigns the same bonding structure to both.
In which substance are covalent bonds broken as it melts?
Melting S I O two requires breaking covalent bonds throughout its network. Melting ice only overcomes attractions between intact water molecules, so B is wrong.

Strong network covalent bonds give a high melting point and the network is generally insoluble in polar solvents. Option B incorrectly assumes a polar solvent dissolves the covalent network.
Consider the following statements. Silicon dioxide has a higher melting point than sulfur dioxide. two. Ammonia has a higher boiling point than phosphine, P H three. Which statements are correct?
S I O two has a giant covalent network, and ammonia forms hydrogen bonds unlike phosphine. Both statements are true, B overlooks the second.

In one breath.
A solid's particles and the attractions between them determine its properties. Use several observed properties together to deduce its structure.
Key ideas.
A regular molecular crystal lattice still contains separate molecules, regular arrangement does not imply a continuous covalent network connecting those molecules.

A giant ionic lattice is a regular three dimensional array of oppositely charged ions. Sodium chloride contains sodium plus and chloride, magnesium oxide contains magnesium two plus and oxide. Strong electrostatic attraction acts throughout each lattice. Neither is made of separate molecules.

A simple molecular lattice has separate molecules in regular positions, held together by intermolecular forces. Solid iodine contains I two molecules held by dispersion forces. Buckminsterfullerene consists of separate C sixty cages, strong covalent bonds are within each cage, but much weaker forces act between cages. Ice contains separate H two O molecules held in an open lattice by hydrogen bonds. The existence of covalent bonds inside a molecule does not make its crystal giant covalent.

A giant molecular, or giant covalent, lattice is one continuous covalent network. In S I O two each silicon bonds to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen bridges two silicon atoms. Diamond has a tetrahedral network with four bonds per carbon and no mobile electrons. Graphite has layers, each carbon bonds to three others, leaving an electron delocalised across a layer, weak forces separate the layers. A giant metallic lattice, such as copper, has positive metal ions attracted to mobile delocalised electrons.
Method.

Identify the particles and the force overcome on melting or boiling. Molecular solids typically melt at lower temperatures because only intermolecular forces are overcome. Giant ionic, metallic and covalent structures require much more energy to disrupt. Ice's hydrogen bonds make its melting point relatively high for a simple molecular solid.

Check conductivity in several states. Metals conduct as solids and liquids through delocalised electrons. Ionic solids do not conduct because ions are fixed, their melts and aqueous solutions conduct through mobile ions. Diamond and S I O two lack mobile charge carriers. Graphite conducts along its layers.

Check solubility. Many ionic solids dissolve in water when hydration stabilises separated ions, but not all do, M G O is only sparingly soluble. Molecular solubility depends on solvent interactions, iodine is poorly soluble in water. Giant covalent networks are generally insoluble. Use solubility with the other tests, never alone.
Worked example.

A brittle solid has a high melting point, does not conduct as a solid, conducts when molten and dissolves in water. Deduce its structure. The high melting point suggests a giant lattice with strong attractions. Conduction only after melting means charged particles are fixed in the solid but mobile in the liquid. These are ions, so the solid has a giant ionic lattice. Water solubility supports this deduction.
Traps.
Trap, Melting iodine breaks its I I bonds. Why it's wrong, Melting separates intact I two molecules. Instead, Name the intermolecular forces overcome.
Trap, A high melting point proves a substance conducts. Why it's wrong, Conduction requires mobile charge carriers. Instead, Ask whether ions or electrons can move in the tested state.

Trap, Every covalent solid is giant covalent. Why it's wrong, C sixty is a crystal of separate covalent molecules. Instead, Decide whether covalent bonds connect the whole lattice or only each molecule.
Exam technique.

When representing an ionic lattice or formula unit, label ions with their correct charges and show their ratio, sodium chloride has sodium plus and chloride in a one to one ratio. Do not draw an isolated covalent molecule in place of these ions.

For Describe, state both the particles and the attractions. For Explain, connect a structural feature to the stated property, say mobile ions or delocalised electrons, not just has charges. For Deduce, cite at least two observations and explain how they support the same structure. Compare solid and molten conductivity before using melting point or solubility as supporting evidence.
